searchText: Bomb delays are entirely hard/time consuming because of coordination, not because of individual work. I have been lobbying for this for a while. If someone takes over EIP editing I'll do it. 😄 I would recommend a more predictable mechanism personally. I do appreciate the argument that having the bomb "creep up" has value because it forces discussion and doesn't allow us to get caught too badly by surprise. Maybe we could do something with the gas limit instead of block times though? Take whatever the voted gas limit is and multiply it by a function of time since the last bomb to figure out the actual gas limit. That way we maintain 12 second blocks (which some apps may incorrectly depend on), but we still slowly throttle the chain until the situation is dealt with. Ah, so gas price would ramp up? I think we just need a dozen more volunteers with throughput similar to mine, and you can retire. Probably, but my main interest is to "make the chain progressively less useful" until a hard fork happens. And I think gas limit decreasing achieves that. slowing block times would an extremely complicated and engineering intensive way to accomplish this I'm generally against introducing a new bomb, but would rather come up with other mechanisms. Agreed. Hence, decreasing gas limit. In theory we could probably do critical updates without a bomb, like if secp256k1 breaks or something. Not adding new EIPs would mean maintenance mode IMO I’m also against fwiw: I think we have a *lot* to ship in the next 3-5 years and very skeptical that we struggle to actually push out new software just because the bomb isn’t there. If we're already shipping software, is delaying the bomb a huge burden? No, but it forces our timelines in an annoying way I don't think that forcing function is annoying at all. It is doing its job. It's purpose (going forward) is to make sure forks happen at least once every y time, so if you hard fork more frequently than that then it is unnecessary and shouldn't ever show up. So lets pick a cadence for releases we like, triple the expected time, and set the bomb to "go off" around then. I personally think 6 months is better. We shouldn't be going 1 year without updates IMO. I'm fine with that, as long as the duration is 1y. I think less creates pressure, and more makes it useless. I don't think it's realistic to push ourselves to fork every 6 months 1 year between hard forks is problematic IMO. Too much time for the ecosystem to stop paying attention, and not enough pressure to release regularly. I could do 9 months, and at 12 months it becomes "annoying" (e.g. equivalent of ~15 sec block times today) I am pretty confident that our hard forks will end up being `bomb_time` apart, and 1 year per fork is too long per fork. agreed that 1 fork year is too few, but 2 is too many IMO I think 2 is too many with our current strategy, but I think forcing 2 per year would force us to pick a different strategy. If _y_ is chosen based on a set of requirements and specification of those requirements then perhaps, but given that at the time the ice age is set there has historically been no idea of what is coming apart from "updates" I'm not a fan of bringing the ice age in to the proof of stake world. The requirement would simply be that we "exercise the release pipeline every `y` time". It is unrelated to whatever features we are building. Yeah, I'm not a fan of using this as a way to force us to change the process when for basically everything we need to ship, quality >> speed, and that we have a lot of "big" things on the roadmap which require custom testing/infra, such as 4844, PBS, stateless, etc. Even if we have nothing to release, I think we should still be exercising the release pipeline regularly. And if features take _y+1_ time then we're updating for the sake of it even though we have a near-future time when we're going to update anyway. I don't want to change the speed at which we develop. I want us to move away from these super monolithic forks. I really don't see the need to have any sort of difficulty bomb whilst we have such a big set of roadmap features. I think the "big features" are the biggest driver of the time, not necessarily the number of EIPs This is why I think there is value in having the bomb "explode" slowly, so we can adjust a bit if needed with minor negative impact (Tim convinced me of this). It is *super* easy to fall into the trap of delaying more and more if you have no external forcing function. I think it is inappropriate to schedule big features for a specific hard fork. We should release them when they are ready. And it's equally easy to ship updates based on the difficulty bomb rather than any code quality metric (see: current situation with the merge). This is part of why I think we should do every 6 months, because that is frequent enough that it forces us to stop targeting hard forks and instead targeting readiness. There is a hard fork ~every 6 months. Whatever is ready by then is included, what isn't is delayed by 6 months. That isn't so long that the delay is devastating if a feature misses the train, but it isn't so frequent that we are spending all of our time releasing. I think in practice you will always want to delay the upgrade for the "big feature": the opportunity cost is just too big If the delay is large, yes. The shorter the delay the less likely you are to try to get a feature into a specific release. It's not worth the coordination cost to ship "a bunch of small features" most of the time, IMO. Also, the way we think about testing does assume EIPs are activated in groups At the extreme, if we had a hard fork every week, no one would care if some big feature misses a hard fork because it'll get in the next one. We want high enough frequency that we get that behavior. I'm not sure what the "release pipeline" even is. New client versions are released roughly monthly, and hard forks are just a subset of that. Release pipeline is ensuring cross client consensus for new features and that end users are upgrading in time. Or is it the co-ordination of forcing everyone to upgrade by a certain time that you want? For regular client updates, we don't need everyone to upgrade. That's just dumping a cost on the entire community, which I would look at as a centralizing force (increased time spent doing upgrades, increased time spent checking for upgrades, all of which come with a disproportionate cost to smaller validators). The coordination cost is: 0. agreeing to which EIPs make it into the fork 1. testing a set of N EIPs together 2. choosing blocks for and running through the fork across testnets 3. advertising (2) to the community, getting folks to update nodes 4. redoing 2-3 for mainnet Post-merge, there is also (5): coordinating this across EL + CLs I think things are much worse if small validators fall out of consensus because they aren't trained to pay attention. Strongly disagree. We have seen over the past 18 months that validators will upgrade, not only for hard forks (Altair) but for performance and bug fixes. But as the burden increases (and as Tim mentions, it will increase significantly when validators need to worry about EL, CL and EL + CL) they are more likely to throw in the towel. I personally feel like we currently put too much emphasis on (1). It definitely needs to happen, but I think it should happen much later in the pipeline. Most EIPs touch unrelated code to each other and naturally don't conflict, so the chance of a bug with a particular pair of EIPs (but not in either individually) is pretty low IMO and should be tested last because it is the hardest to do. One of the many things that I think could potentially be improved by us releasing more frequently (forcing us to stop testing EIP batches, and instead test individual EIPs). I think this is a bit special right now because The Merge is such a hot topic. Also, validators are not the only ecosystem participants we care about, we want all node operators to update appropriately. (Somewhat orthogonal to this, but if we did end up with an ice age I'd prefer it to be a hard stop at a given block height rather than a function like we have with the difficulty bomb. Or the CL can continue as is and the EL can drop a fraction of payloads, or something. Whatever ends up being chosen should avoid the mess that variable consensus layer block times produces). Yeah. I think we all agree on this. I like gas limit decreases personally, but I agree that block time is the wrong target. Validators are the only ecosystem participants who can impact the chain's progression. But fatigue is real, and upgrading for upgrading's sake (_i.e._ upgrades without any changes in functionality just to push back an arbitrary difficulty bomb) will get old quick. My suspicion is that we have a long way to go before we are at "bomb only" updates, assuming we have a healthy release process (more healthy than currently) and the bomb is predictable. If 1 eth is staked that’s understandable I suspect a few updates a year on a $70,000+ amount is reasonable Which surely makes the bomb extraneous. I think without the bomb we'll fall into the monolithic release trap, where we have 2 years of no forks then one super fork that changes a ton of stuff. With a bomb. So we're back to the bomb forcing the size of updates, even though a bomb pushback should be a totally separate update to a feature release.

I think that my fundamental problem here is that we're leaning on the bomb rather than have any sort of mature development process.  It isn't impossible to have a plan, a roadmap, lists of features that we aim to put in the next 3-4 releases and management of said features such that they can be built in reasonable (6-12 month) chunks.  Yes they can move around, but that's true regardless of the presence of a bomb and having the flexibility allows us to be dynamic with releases rather than tied to an arbitrary beat.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
An analogy: if you are trying to diet, it is far easier to not buy unhealthy groceries than it is to not eat unhealthy food that is already in the house.

I think the same is true for individual humans and groups of humans, it is much harder to "do the right thing" in the moment than it is to setup the situation such that doing the wrong thing is hard.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: In this case, I think a bomb of sorts is a way to setup the situation such that it is harder for our future selves to make a bad "just this one time" decision in the future.

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content: By that argument though it's simple for the "just this one time" decision to be ditching the difficulty bomb, so we're going to have to grow up one day.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Ditching the bomb requires a release, and it wouldn't solve the "in the moment problem", it would only "solve" the future problem.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: If you are craving for a candy bar but don't have any in the house, ordering some for delivery in two weeks won't help, and is easier to resist doing than ignoring a candy bar that is right in front of you.

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content: Or we could be grown ups and have impulse control (or, spooling back from the analogy, a roadmap with release milestones).

excerpts.author: sky.cactus

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content:
I "upgraded" to the latest release (which was in beta at the time, if I remember correctly) on my laptop a month or two ago.  I have received near-daily updates of software since then.  I couldn't even tell you when in April it was officially released.  So I think that it's largely (outside of the introduction of a new kernel) irrelevant in terms of it's regularity.

(And now I'll definitely stop talking about it.)

excerpts.author: samwilsn
excerpts.content:
I think that would be roughly equivalent to how client releases would work. In Ubuntu, generally the versions of constituent software are pinned before the OS releases, and only minor updates are permitted (security/bugfixes) after that.

In our release cycle, a hardfork is analogous to a new OS version, but clients would still be free to release minor changes between forks.

excerpts.author: alexssd7fp
excerpts.content: Ubuntu makes a release every three months, it's just that they do not get long term support (LTS) from Canonical. As there is no such meaning as LTS and non-LTS in Ethereum, I don't think it is applicable here. Also, my personal opinion, but two years is way too much for crypto.

excerpts.author: alexssd7fp
excerpts.content:
Totally on board with <@301186049323958275> here. Scheduled upgrades will be so much better on long term for the ecosystem, as people will know in advance when they will need to upgrade.

I never was a fan of "when it's ready we will deploy it" approach, as it makes things unpredictable. (Shoutout to the Merge)

excerpts.author: alexssd7fp
excerpts.content: Plus Ethereum node runners will develop a habit of periodic network upgrades, which will make the HF coordination easier in the future.

excerpts.author: bridge-bot
excerpts.content:
<timbeiko> I used to think that, but now feel pretty strongly that “getting the most important thing in” is much more important than providing an extra bit of predictibility, at least in the short/medium term when we have huge things to ship. 

Maybe once Ethereum is in “maintenance mode” we’ll get more predictibility, but right now I’d focus over making sure we deliver the most important things, rather than optimizing “how neatly we deliver them” from a process perspective.

excerpts.author: alexssd7fp
excerpts.content: Scheduled forks every 6 months + in-depth preparation that would include research on what Ethereum infrastructure providers need to change in order to keep their operations working is what I would #want #want #want to see in Ethereum.

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: Also you can't do fixed scheduling and fixed scope.  The merge has a quite big minimal possible scope (what we're delivering). Same thing applies to a lot of EIPs - it's not easy to split the research, development and testing down into something that fits into a fixed schedule.  And you can't just do the research ahead of time or you find it's unworkable when development starts.

excerpts.author: alexssd7fp
excerpts.content: Kind of remembers me the situation with the EIP-1559, where we were told that "technically we just need to upgrade our node", but in fact we had to rewrite a lot of stuff on our end to be prepared for the London fork 😄

excerpts.author: .paulharris
excerpts.content: you can do fixed scheduling and fix scope if quality is negotiable... which it isn't...

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: I'm a big fan of small, regular releases but that's very different to fixed schedule.

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: Also a fan in theory, but when I look at things like the merge, sharding, statelessness, proposer/builder separation, etc. it's clear none of these are "small" and having a process that's optimized for that might mean we ship smaller things at the expense of bigger/murkier ones which are more important

excerpts.author: alexssd7fp
excerpts.content: I disagree. Ethereum is a hundred-billion-dollar platform, and stability, predictability, and security - must be a #1 priority.

excerpts.author: ajsutton
excerpts.content: Yep - that's exactly my thinking as well.  "Small" doesn't always fit into the same size box.
